messages.subject: upscaling of diversity
messages.body_plain:
Dear all

This is my first post to the list so i apologise if I approach a topic =
already covered.=20

=20

I am currently writing up my PhD on the ancient woodlands of greater =
Manchester, as part of this work I am looking at ground beetle =
assemblages and the effect of isolation and fragmentation on both =
species composition and abundance.=20

Within the constraints of my project I was only able to sample two =
locations within each chosen woodland, roughly covering the edge and =
core zones. My sampling design constituted of pitfall trapping in a =
standard 3x3 grid using methanol to kill and preserve specimens. These =
traps were emptied every second week for a year culminating in the =
capture of over 13,000 individuals and 49 species.=20

=20

What I want to look at is the potential species diversity for the whole =
site at the edge and the core. Do any of you know how it would be =
possible to upsize the species number to be proportional to the total =
woodland area rather than the specific locations that I surveyed. This =
would be simple if I was looking at the  number of individuals as I =
would multiply that number by the amount of times the sample area fitted =
into the whole woodland. The calculations for species number represents =
a different problem.=20

=20

I would greatly appreciate any direction and help in this matter even if =
it is to simply say that it can not be done.=20

=20

Cheers

=20

Ben Allen

=20

Department of Environmental and Geographical Sciences

MMU

=20

ben.a...@btinternet.com

b.a...@mmu.ac.uk=20

messages.subject: Analysis of data from a single point transect
messages.subject_clean: Analysis of data from a single point transect
messages.body_plain:
Hi Cindy,

I'm cc'ing my answer to the list, so it will be there in the archives ready for
the next person who asks.

On Wed, 28 Jan 2004 23:45:26 -0400, Cindy Staicer wrote:

> >For some time I have been trying to figure out if DISTANCE can be
> >used to calculate a density for a given bird species at a SINGLE
> >point count. I have data for several species.

> >I have been working through the 2001 edition of Introduction to
> >Distance Sampling and the on-line manual, and I have searched the
> >archives but I haven't noticed an answer to my question.

Absolutely it can, just as it can from a single line transect (see the Ducknest
and Beercan example projects as examples).

There are two cases when you might want to do this:

The first is (as for the beercan example) when the surveyed strip *is* the whole
study area.  This can happen for simulation exercises like the beercan study,
where they layed out cans in a strip 200 meters long and 40 meters wide (I think
that was it), and then surveyed a line down the middle with truncation distance
20 meters.  You can think of the usual distance sampling estimator of abundance
as having two parts. First fit a detection function and use this to estimate the
average probabilty of detection within the strip (p).  Use this to estimate the
number of animals in the surveyed area (as number seen divided by p).  Second,
"scale up" this estimate to the number of animals in the whole study area.  In
the case where the surveyed area *is* the study area you don't need the second
part.  So the only source of uncertainty in the abundance estimate comes from
estimating the detection function.  How do you tell this to Distance?  One way
is under Model Definition | Variance | Encounter rate variance, click the option
to "Assume distribution is Poisson, with overdispersion factor" and then enter
0.  This will give you no encounter rate variance -- what you want.  I think
this is correct -- no doubt someone on the list will correct me if they
disagree.  If you want a bootstrap estimate of variance, I guess the thing to do
is to bootstrap by observation.

The second case would be when you have a study area larger than your single
point or line, but for some reason your design was to have only one replicate.
Clearly, this is not a good design, but I have seen it on several occasions
(ideally, you'd like 20 or more lines or points).  In this case, you do want
variation in encounter rate to enter the calculations.  But you have only one
line, so the default option under Model Definition | Variance | Encounter rate
variance to "Estimate variance empirically" is not going to work (this uses the
between-line variation in encounter rate).  So instead, you're going to have to
either assume the variation is Poisson (the second option), or Poisson with some
overdispersion (Buckland et al. 2001, page 242 cite Burnham et al. 1980 as
providing a rationale for values for overdispersion in the range 1.5-3 and in
the analysis of duck nest data (Table 8.4) got values around 1.7).  Assuming
some number is not very satisfactory, as it will make a huge difference to the
final variance estimate and confidence limits, but you have no option.  Using
temporal variation in encounter rate if you have repeat visits to the point will
certainly underestimate the variance.

Hope this helps,

 - Len

--
Len Thomas, Co-ordinator, Distance Development Project
Research Unit for Wildlife Population Assessment
Centre for Research into Environmental and Ecological Modelling
The Observatory, University of St Andrews, Scotland KY16 9LZ

messages.subject: Re: Analysis of data from a single point transect
messages.subject_clean: Analysis of data from a single point transect
messages.body_plain:
>> > >For some time I have been trying to figure out if DISTANCE can be
>> > >used to calculate a density for a given bird species at a SINGLE
>> > >point count. I have data for several species.

I would add two points to Len's response.

1. If the design comprises a single point, only in very unusual
circumstances would you get a large enough sample size to get an estimate
with reasonable precision.  I can't envisage a real survey in which this
option would be useful.  One reason for having many points, randomly
positioned (or a randomly-positioned grid of points) is that, on average,
the density of objects in the popn (whether detected or not) increases
linearly, as required.  This is unlikely to be the case for a single
point, so that your estimate may be poor even if you have lots of
detections.

2. It is not clear from your query whether you really do have just one
point in your design, or whether you have many, but want to estimate
density separately for each point.  In the latter case, you can select a
common detection function (or a common detection function model, but with
covariates that vary by point or object), but estimate density by sample
(point in this case).  This can potentially be useful, but for most
species, you are likely to get an estimate of zero at many of the points.

Steve Buckland

messages.subject: Observer variability
messages.body_plain:
On Fri, 30 Jan 2004 08:37:32 -0700, Robin E Russell wrote:

> >Hi- I'm new to the list and I checked the archives but I didn't see this
> >question addressed directly, but I didn't want to send an irrelevant
> >message to several hundred people on first try.  Anyway, my question is
> >regarding point count data.  I have one particular observer who is
> >misjudging distances, however, I believe the problem is concentrated
> >between the first and second bins.  (The bins are 0-10, 10-25, 25-50,
> >50-75, 75-100) Is there a problem with combining the first two bins to
> >compensate for this error?  I know this means there will only be 4 bins and
> >therefore I may have problems with adjustment terms and lack of GOF tests.
> >I also know the new Distance book will discuss a methods of compensating if
> >you have some accurate estimates for the observer.  In the meantime what do
> >you think of the above solution?

> >Thanks

> >Robin E. Russell

Hi Robin,

Seems like a reasonable question for archiving on the list, so I've forwarded
this message there.

There's no problem with combining the two bins -- indeed that's exactly what you
need to do in this case.  However, it's probably going to have a bad effect on
the variance of the estimate of h(0) -- it will be harder for the fitting
algorithm to tell what the slope of the pdf is at 0 distance when it has such
large inner bins.    No real alternative however.

You had the right approach in having two small inner bins, and increasing bin
width with distance from the point.  Allows one more scope to test for problems
and look for a shoulder in the detection function.

I wouldn't worry too much about constraints on adjustment terms and GOF tests as
unless you have lots of data or a spiked detection function you're unlikely to
want lots of adjustment terms (a good general rule).  Your main problem with GOF
tests will be lack of ability to look for a shoulder in the detection function.

Did you consider going to exact distances in future, or at least tightening up
on distance measurements using a laser rangefinder?  For many point transect
studies, detections are mostly aural (of birds singing in forest, for example).
In reasonably open forest one may estimate distance by first guessing which
tree, bush, group of trees, etc the bird was singing from, and then estimating
the distance to that object.  Laser rangefinders would remove the uncertainty
involved in the second part of this process.  They may be of most use for the
closest birds detected, but then these are also the ones where you need the best
accuracy.  Just a thought (may not be practical in your study) ...

 - Len

--

messages.subject: questions (new user) re: convergence failure & cluster size bias
messages.subject_clean: questions (new user) re: convergence failure & cluster size bias
messages.body_plain:
Greetings

I am new to the listserv (& new to DISTANCE).  I have briefly perused
recent archives & help & have not seen these topics - if answers to my
questions are already present, please excuse my overlooking them & feel
free to point me in the right direction.  Also, please reply offline to
jcar...@usd.edu unless you feel the answer would be useful to others.
I'd be happy to compile answers ONLY IF others would find it useful.

I my analyses, I have several times run into 2 warnings: 'convergence
failure' and 'size bias adjustment has increased expected cluster size'.
I am wondering about the seriousness of these issues as far as affecting
density & detectability results.  Someone with more experience than me
with DISTANCE has suggested that truncating especially distant outliers
is a way to overcome the convergence failure warning.  I've found this
to be true (& results hardly change) BUT is this an appropriate way of
dealing with this warning?

Thanks in advance for any helpful suggestions.

Cheers,

Jay
